newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Ukraine warns electricity consumers of cut-off.
newsitem.headline: Ukraine warns electricity consumers of cut-off.

text.p: Ukraine has given customers who owe almost $2 billion for electricity three days to pay up or be cut off and plans to do the same to rake in an even larger figure in unpaid gas bills, government officials said on Thursday.

"The situation is very difficult and it has been going on for a couple of years. We are talking about constant, systematic unpaid bills," Valentyn Bondarenko, Deputy Electricity Minister, told a news conference.
"The government decided this week to cut off all customers from the electricity grid on June 1," Bondarenko added. "Whoever doesn't pay for electricity -- won't get it."
Ukrainians owe 3.5 billion hryvnias ($1.88 billion) for electricity while the industry owes its creditors 4.4 billion hryvnias ($2.36 billion).
Ukraine's annual electricity output stood last year at 300 billion kilowatt hours from 200 billion kilowatt hours in 1990.

The former Soviet republic's 41 thermal power stations, some of them with ageing equipment and low efficiency, produce 51 percent of its electricity, while five nuclear plants including Chernobyl power station produce 45 percent.
The rest comes from six hydrostations, built in the 1930s under Soviet industrialisation on the Dnieper river.
Bondarenko said some customers -- including hospitals, childrens' homes and homes for the sick and elderly and military units on combat duty, would be excluded from the order.
This year 12,000 customers, mostly enterprises, have been cut off from the electricity grid. Bondarenko said his ministry was insisting that tariffs be increased by 30 percent.
Mykhailo Kovalko, head of the State Oil and Gas Committee told the same news conference that the government had been preparing the same order on unpaid gas bills.

"Unfortunately the problem of unpaid gas bills has not been resolved. The tendency is for it to continue to grow," Kovalko said, adding that 4.4 billion hryvnias ($2.36 billion) in unpaid debts had been amassed since the start of 1995.
He said 2,000 enterprises had already been cut off.

"The previous, old debts will not be forgiven. We'll draw up timetables for payments with terms between six months and a year," he said. "There is a need for urgent steps. Gas is a commodity and should be paid for."
Some commentators were sceptical about the government moves.

"Let's see how strong the government's intentions are," said Alla Yeremenko, energy commentator at Zerkalo Nedeli weekly. "The government took the same decision two years ago and last year too. You see the results -- the debts only grew."
"The difference is that we used to say -- those who don't pay might be cut off," said Taras Freyuk, head of Ukrgaz state company. "Now we say -- those will be cut off. For sure."
